chunk_findings.detail: The new code calls `shlex.quote(note)` but never imports `shlex`. `command_line` imports every dependency it uses locally — `import shutil` at the top of the body and `from ..infra.paths import launch_parent, launch_python` in the branch — and the diff adds no `import shlex` anywhere in the changed region. Given that `shutil.which("ddflow")` is resolved via a local `import shutil`, the module clearly does not rely on a top-level import for this helper, so `shlex` is undefined here. Input that demonstrates it: any invocation, e.g. `ddflow hooks install` (or simply calling `_commit_invocation()`/`_msg_invocation()`), reaches `note = shlex.quote(...)` and raises `NameError: name 'shlex' is not defined`, so `command_line` never returns a hook line at all — the entire fail-open hook/launcher generation is dead before the shell text is produced. The fix is to add `import shlex` alongside `import shutil` (or at module scope).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py :: command_line (the new `note = shlex.quote(...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded-launcher probe only tests that the recorded path exists and has the execute bit set; it does not test that the launcher can actually be executed. A very common "dangling" form is a pip/uv console script whose shebang points at an interpreter that has since been removed (e.g. `#!/home/u/…/python` when that env was deleted or upgraded): the script file is still present and executable, so `[ -x "…/ddflow" ]` succeeds, the `then` branch runs `exec "…/ddflow" hooks check-commit "$@"`, the kernel returns ENOENT for the missing interpreter, the shell exits 126/127, and `command_line(..., exec_=True)` therefore blocks every `git commit`. This is exactly the failure the change claims to prevent ("the venv was deleted, the tool uninstalled"), and it is not caught by the probe. A probe that also validates the executable (e.g. `[ -x "$launcher" ] && "$launcher" --version >/dev/null 2>&1`, or checking the shebang target) is needed to make the fallback actually fail open for a present-but-broken launcher.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py :: command_line (probe `[ -x "{script}" ]`)

chunk_findings.detail: `check_command` sets `fallback=_on_path()` (`shutil.which("ddflow") is not None`) unconditionally, but the ability to fall back to `ddflow` on PATH belongs to the *recorded line*, not to the machine. Per the module's own docstring, lines matched by `_LEGACY_EXEC`/`_LEGACY_PYPATH` are "lines written before the fallback existed" and have neither a PATH fallback nor fail-open behaviour. Input: a project with a pre-existing pre-commit hook installed by an older ddflow, whose recorded `exec "/old/venv/bin/python"` path has been deleted, while `ddflow` happens to be on the doctor's PATH. `recorded_paths` takes the legacy branch, `_gone` reports the missing path, and `check_command` returns `Dangling(..., fallback=True)`, so `render()` prints "… it falls back to `ddflow` on PATH for now". That is false for this hook: it has no PATH fallback, so it still `exec`s the missing interpreter and *blocks* the commit — the exact B-dangling-precommit-hook symptom the doctor is supposed to surface. Symmetrically, for a legacy hook with no `ddflow` on PATH the message says "the hook fails open and the check is skipped", which is also untrue for legacy lines (they fail the commit). The fallback flag (and the message chosen from it) should be derived from whether the line contains the `_PROBE` fallback form, not from `_on_path()`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/launchers.py:67-70 (`check_command`)

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP check splits `PYTHONPATH` on `os.pathsep` but then only ever inspects the *first* entry, both when testing for `ddflow/__init__.py` and when building the reported missing path. Input: `.mcp.json` with `"env": {"PYTHONPATH": "/opt/deps:/repo/src"}` where `ddflow` is importable only via `/repo/src`. The code tests `/opt/deps/ddflow/__init__.py`, does not find it, and reports "the ddflow MCP entry in .mcp.json records /opt/deps/ddflow, which no longer exists", a false positive even though the server launches fine. Since multi-entry `PYTHONPATH` is ordinary, the check should test each pathsep segment (or the whole string via the interpreter's resolution) rather than hard-coding the first.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/launchers.py:check_mcp (`root.split(os.pathsep)[0]`)

chunk_findings.detail: This test asserts the fail-open path (`returncode == 0` and `"ddflow: not found" in r.stderr`) but, unlike every sibling fail-open test (`test_a_dead_recorded_launcher_does_not_fail_the_commit`, `test_the_skip_is_one_line_per_hook`, `test_a_dead_recorded_launcher_falls_back_to_ddflow_on_path`, all of which take `bare_path`), it does **not** take the `bare_path` fixture, so the ambient `PATH` is left intact. The command under test is `E.command_line(CH.MARKER)` with only the *recorded absolute paths* rewritten to `/nonexistent-ddflow-venv/...`; the runtime resolver in that command line falls back to `command -v ddflow` on `PATH` (exactly the behaviour the other tests exercise via `test_a_dead_recorded_launcher_falls_back_to_ddflow_on_path`). In any environment where the project's own `ddflow` entry point is on `PATH` — the normal case when the suite is run from an installed/dev venv, which is precisely why the git-hook tests were given `bare_path` — `sh -c line` resolves the real `ddflow` and executes it instead of taking the fail-open branch, so the line `ddflow: not found` is never written to stderr and the assertion fails (or becomes dependent on whatever the real hook command happens to print/return). The test needs `bare_path` (or an otherwise-emptied `PATH`) to be hermetic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_dangling_hook.py:230 (test_a_claude_hook_command_fails_open_when_ddflow_is_gone)

chunk_findings.detail: The block reports any dangling launcher returned by `LA.findings(repo)`, and `data["dangling"]` is populated from the same object. If `launchers.findings()` yields a one-shot iterable (generator) rather than a list, `if dangling:` is always true and the `join(...)` consumes it, so `data["dangling"]` is always `[]` while `message` still prints the lines — an inconsistency between the machine-readable field and the human message. This is unresolvable from part 1 alone (the implementation of `findings()` is in a part not shown), so it is flagged only as a low-confidence interaction, not a demonstrated failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:676 (hooks status dangling block)

chunk_findings.detail: `recorded_paths` extracts a path from a probe that may be written as `[ -x "<path>" ]` (the regex `_PROBE` explicitly matches both `-x` and `-f`), but the existence decision is made solely with `os.path.exists` in `_gone`. For an `-x` probe these two tests are not equivalent: a recorded launcher that still exists but is no longer executable (e.g. someone ran `chmod -x .venv/bin/ddflow`, or the repo lives on an NFS/vfat mount with `noexec`, or the bit was lost restoring a backup) makes `[ -x ... ]` fail, so the hook takes its fallback/fail-open branch and the check is silently skipped — exactly the situation this module claims to report — yet `check_command` sees a path that exists and returns `None`, so `doctor` and `hooks status` stay quiet. To be faithful to the intent ("a check that quietly stopped running must still be REPORTED") the `-x` probe needs `os.access(p, os.X_OK)` (and `-f` needs `os.path.isfile`), not bare existence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/launchers.py:_gone / check_command (probe `-x` vs `os.path.exists`)

chunk_findings.detail: `check_command` sets `fallback=_on_path()` purely from the environment, regardless of whether the command line actually contains a fallback branch. For a line matched by the legacy path (the module's own docstring: "the older lines that had no fallback"), there is no `command -v ddflow` branch at all — the shell simply `exec`s the recorded script, and if that script is gone the git hook exits non-zero and blocks the commit. Input: a pre-commit hook written before this change containing `exec "/old/venv/bin/python" ...` (or the `_LEGACY_PYPATH` form) where `/old/venv` has been deleted, with `ddflow` installed on PATH. `check_command` returns a `Dangling` with `fallback=True`, and `render()` prints "…it falls back to `ddflow` on PATH for now", telling the user a check is still running when in fact nothing runs it — the opposite of what this module exists to make visible. `fallback` should be derived from the command text (presence of the fallback branch/probe), not only from `shutil.which`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_gone` was broadened from "path does not exist" to "path does not exist **or is not executable**" (e.g. a launcher that exists but lost its `+x` bit, exactly the case exercised by `test_a_launcher_that_is_no_longer_executable_is_reported`). `_gone` now returns such a path in `missing`, but the only user-facing rendering, `Dangling.__str__`, still asserts `f"{self.where} records {gone}, which no longer exists; ..."`. Concrete input: a hook recording `/path/ddflow` where `/path/ddflow` exists with mode 0644. `check_command` returns `Dangling(..., missing=('/path/ddflow',), ...)`, and `ddflow doctor` / `hooks status` then print "records /path/ddflow, which no longer exists" — factually false and self-contradictory (`ls` shows the file). Before this change `missing` could only contain paths that truly did not exist, so the wording was accurate; the change silently invalidated it. The message should distinguish "missing" from "not executable" (e.g. "is gone, or is no longer executable"), otherwise the new non-executable detection reports itself with a misleading line.
